title: The Pain of Leaving Your Team for Another Opportunity
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article grapples with the genuine tension leaders feel when weighing a new opportunity against loyalty to the team they built. It argues there are no perfectly clean answers, only leaders who work hard to depart as a 'good leaver': committing to a real transition plan, documenting critical knowledge, prepping a successor, and maintaining important relationships regardless of the formal notice period. The piece emphasizes honest, direct communication about the decision without bad-mouthing the organization or over-apologizing, framing how a leader exits as a lasting reflection of their character and legacy.
points: Leaving a team leaders helped build creates real, unavoidable tension between loyalty and opportunity.
There are no clean answers, only leaders who choose to depart well or poorly.
Good leavers commit real time to a transition plan, documentation, and successor prep before leaving.
Honest, direct communication about the reasons for leaving matters more than avoiding the conversation.
How a leader exits becomes a lasting reflection of their character and legacy.
quotes: Good leaders feel a deep responsibility for the team they have helped to create.
When leaders choose to exit, their goal must be to depart as a “good leaver,” respecting the needs of the organization and team as much as their own.
Good leavers depart on good terms. Regardless of the official notice period, they commit the time to close the books on the past before moving on to the future.
They don’t apologize for leaving, but instead thank people for their contribution and support.
Good leavers, like good leaders, are in short supply. They shouldn’t be.
